Cannot
kăn'ŏt
v. (the negative of can; in Scripture the word that marks a real moral inability, not a mere difficulty)
A fusion of can and not, written as two words into the eighteenth century and as one thereafter. The Authorized Version prints it both ways.

Biblical Definition

Cannot is one of the most doctrinally weighted words in the New Testament, because Scripture repeatedly says of fallen man not that he will not but that he cannot. “They that are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom 8:8), which follows from the verse before it: the carnal mind is enmity against God, is not subject to His law, “neither indeed can be”. “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1Co 15:50) — the body as it now is, mortal and corruptible, is unfit for the world to come and must be changed. “As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me” (Joh 15:4). And “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24), where the impossibility is not of effort but of nature: two absolute masters cannot both be absolute. In every case the inability is moral, not physical — the sinner is not prevented by a chain but disinclined by a nature, which is why he is fully responsible for what he cannot do.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) treats cannot as the compound of can and not, expressing want of power or of ability, and notes that it is written as one word or as two.

expand to see more

CANNOT. This word is usually written as one word, but is properly two, can and not, expressing inability.

CAN, v.i. To be able; to have sufficient strength, means or moral power.

Note. The distinction between natural and moral inability is of great moment in theology; a man cannot fly, and a man cannot love what he hates, but not in the same manner.

Note. How can ye, being evil, speak good things? Matt. xii.

Key Scripture

Rom 8:8 — "So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God."

1Co 15:50 — "Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption."

Joh 15:4 — "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me."

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Modern Corruption

The Bible's cannot is softened into finds it difficult, which quietly denies total depravity and makes regeneration an assistance rather than a resurrection.

expand to see more

Almost every departure from Reformed soteriology can be traced to the handling of this one word. Semi-Pelagian and Arminian schemes must read cannot as a strong will not, leaving the fallen will with enough residual power to cooperate with grace. Scripture will not bend that way. Paul writes that the carnal mind “is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7), and John reports the Lord saying “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). Total depravity does not mean men are as wicked as they could be; it means the whole man — mind, affections, will — is fallen, and that the disability reaches the very faculty that would have to choose.

The old distinction preserves both truths. A man's inability is moral, not natural: he is not shackled, he is disinclined; he has every faculty required to come to Christ and no desire to use them. That is why the inability excuses no one — a man who cannot love what he hates is not thereby innocent — and why the remedy must be a new nature rather than better arguments. Eze 36:26 promises a new heart, and Eph 2:5 says God quickened us when we were dead. Not helped; quickened. The cannot of Rom 8:8 is what makes monergism necessary and what makes it glorious.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English can + not; rendering Greek ou dunamai (G3756 with G1410), not to be able, and Hebrew lo yakol, he is not able.

expand to see more

Greek ou dunamai — not to be able; the flat negative of power, used at Rom 8:8, Joh 15:4, and 1Co 15:50.

Greek oude dunatai — “neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7); the added oude forecloses the possibility as well as the fact.

Hebrew lo yakol — he is not able; used of Joseph's brethren, who “could not speak peaceably unto him” (Gen 37:4) — a moral inability if ever there was one.

Joh 6:44 — oudeis dunatai elthein, “no man can come to me”; the drawing of the Father is the necessary condition.

Eph 2:1, 5 — nekrous, dead; the state that makes the cannot intelligible and the quickening necessary.

Usage

"“They that are in the flesh cannot please God” — inability of nature, not of opportunity."

"“Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom” — the mortal body must be changed, not merely improved."

"“Ye cannot serve God and mammon” — two absolute masters cannot both be absolute."
